blocks.content: Memory, unlike CPU, is an incompressible resource, a container cannot simply be "slowed down" when it runs out, exceeding a memory limit always results in the container being killed outright.
Memory requests are expressed in binary units, Mi (mebibytes) and Gi (gibibytes) are the most common, 256Mi or 1Gi are typical, real-world values you will see constantly in manifests.

blocks.alt: Familiar binary units, seen constantly in real manifests

blocks.content: 2. Summed by the Scheduler, Just Like CPU
blocks.text: 2. Summed by the Scheduler, Just Like CPU

blocks.content: Exactly the same mechanism covered for CPU Requests applies here, the scheduler sums up memory requests across a node's existing Pods, and only places a new Pod there if enough memory genuinely remains available.

blocks.alt: The same summing logic, applied to memory instead of CPU

blocks.content: This is the defining, opposite characteristic from CPU: memory cannot be "slowed down," a process either has the memory it needs or it does not, there is no equivalent of throttling for memory at all.

blocks.alt: No equivalent of throttling exists for memory at all

blocks.content: This is one of the most commonly tested facts about Kubernetes resource management: exceeding a CPU limit results in throttling, a soft, recoverable consequence, exceeding a memory limit results in an OOMKill, a hard, immediate termination, the two resources behave fundamentally differently under pressure.

blocks.alt: Throttled versus killed outright, the single most important asymmetry to remember

blocks.content: A common pattern sets the memory limit noticeably above the request, giving a container some real headroom for occasional spikes, while still capping it at a level that protects the rest of the node from being starved if something genuinely goes wrong.

blocks.alt: Headroom above the baseline request, still capped at a safe ceiling

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Memory is measured in Mi/Gi and, unlike CPU, is incompressible, there is no equivalent of throttling, a container over its memory limit is simply OOMKilled.
This CPU-versus-memory asymmetry (throttled versus killed) is one of the most important, frequently tested facts about how Kubernetes manages resources.
